Chapter 7: The Role of Generosity — Cultivating a Giving Mindset.
When you think about generosity, what comes to mind? For a lot of folks, it’s all about money—giving what you have, maybe writing a check or dropping spare change in a donation box. But real generosity? It's so much bigger than that.
It's a mindset—a way of looking at yourself, and your place in the world, that goes way beyond dollars and cents. And when it comes to managing money, being generous isn’t just about how much you give. It’s about your intention, and that habit of looking past your own needs to see the bigger picture.
Teaching generosity, especially to kids, lays the groundwork for empathy, gratitude, and a real sense of connection with others.
One of the simplest, most hands-on ways to build this mindset is with something like a giving jar. Ever tried it? Even dropping a few coins in for a local cause, or using it to buy a treat for a friend, can do wonders.
It’s not just about what goes in the jar—it’s about letting kids choose where their money goes, and actually seeing the difference they can make. That feeling? It’s powerful. It helps them realize that anyone, no matter how small, can make an impact.
If you’re wondering how to help kids—and honestly, ourselves—cultivate a giving mindset, here are a few simple steps:
First, involve them in choosing who to help. Maybe it’s picking a local animal shelter, supporting a neighborhood project, or helping out a friend who’s having a hard time. Let them decide, and you’ll see them light up with a sense of purpose.
Next, share stories. Talk about the real ways donations help, whether that’s through stories from your own life, or things happening right in your community. These stories stick with us, and make the act of giving feel real—not just an abstract idea.
And don’t forget to model generosity yourself. Tell your kids why you give, and how it feels when you support a cause you care about. When you open up about your own experiences, you’re showing them that giving is a natural, joyful part of life.
Now, generosity isn’t only about money. Sometimes, the most meaningful gifts are time, attention, or simple acts of kindness. Volunteering as a family, or making cards for neighbors down the street—these things can become habits, and help us look for ways to help wherever we go.
Over time, practicing generosity builds a sense of abundance, not scarcity. Kids start to see that giving doesn’t mean having less—instead, it’s about creating more meaning and connection. And that’s such an important lesson, especially in a world that’s always pushing us to want more, buy more, compete more.
Families who make giving a regular habit often find that it brings them closer together. Working toward a goal, side by side, creates a sense of pride and shared purpose. It opens up conversations about what matters to each person, and the kind of difference they want to make in the world.
So, here’s the key takeaway: building a habit of generosity is at the heart of healthy money management. When families and kids make giving a regular part of life, they build empathy, gratitude, and a deep sense of purpose—qualities that last a lifetime, and reach far beyond anything money can buy.
